title: Guests with news
hook: angels visit Ibrahim, he hurries to feed them, and his wife laughs at the news of a son

segments.voice: Yesterday: khalil, the friend of Allah, the name Ibrahim carries. Your line was a friend listens. Did you get a minute to talk, and to listen back? Day thirty-eight.

You know the moment. The doorbell rings and you weren't expecting anyone. Somewhere in your head a quick inventory starts: is there anything in the fridge? Is the couch covered in laundry? Ibrahim, peace be upon him, gets that doorbell. Strangers arrive at his tent. They say peace, and he says peace back. He doesn't know who they are. He doesn't ask what they want. The Qur'an says he slipped away to his household, quietly, and came back with a whole roasted calf. Not a snack. A feast, for people he'd never met. And then something strange happens. The guests don't eat. Their hands don't reach for the food. Today: the guests with news.
screen: `STRANGERS AT THE TENT.` → `A WHOLE ROASTED CALF.` → `THEIR HANDS DON'T MOVE.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an tells this story twice, in Surah Hud and in Surah adh-Dhariyat, and each telling adds a detail. Start with the speed. Surah Hud says he did not delay. Adh-Dhariyat says he went to his family quietly, so the guests wouldn't feel like a burden, and brought a fat calf and set it close to them. Then he says, gently, won't you eat? That's the whole of hospitality in two verses: hurry, don't make a fuss about it, put the best you have within reach. The Qur'an calls them the honored guests of Ibrahim, and the honor starts with the host. Then the turn. They don't eat, and Ibrahim feels a flicker of fear. In his world, a guest who refused your food might mean you harm. They say, don't be afraid. They're messengers, angels, sent on to the people of Lut. And they have news for this house. His wife is standing nearby. The Qur'an doesn't name her; Muslim tradition knows her as Sarah. She laughs. She says, how can I bear a child, an old woman, with a husband this old? And the angels answer, are you amazed at the command of Allah? A son is coming, Ishaq, and after him a grandson, Ya'qub. Commentators have long asked why she laughed, and they don't agree: at the surprise, at relief, at the sheer impossibility. The text leaves it open. Jews and Christians tell this visit too, at the oaks of Mamre in Genesis. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ made the host's side of it part of faith: a hadith in Bukhari says whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let them honor their guest. Ibrahim fed strangers before he knew they carried good news. The feeding came first.
screen: `HE DID NOT DELAY.` · `THE HONORED GUESTS OF IBRAHIM.` · `THE GUESTS DON'T EAT.` · `SHE LAUGHS AT THE NEWS.` · then, large: `HONOR YOUR GUEST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feed someone today, quickly and well. Settle, and breathe. Picture the people you'll cross paths with between now and tonight. A roommate, a coworker, a kid, a neighbor, the person who always brings snacks and never gets any. Pick one. Now picture what you could put within their reach. A coffee. Half your lunch. A plate saved for later. Nothing fancy; the calf was the best Ibrahim had, and yours can be the best you have today, even if it's a granola bar. If you pray, you can ask for an open hand. The bell holds the time.
Guests with news. Strangers fed before anyone knew who they were, and a laugh at a promise that sounded impossible. Today's word.
Your line: hurry to the guest. Today, when someone walks in, even into a chat, offer something before they have to ask. Day thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Hospitality is a deep part of Muslim life: guests are welcomed with food and drink as soon as they arrive, often before any question of why they came, and many Muslims point to the hadith about honoring the guest as the reason.

fork.setup: you're Ibrahim. strangers arrive and greet you with peace. you don't know who they are. what do you do?
options: ask them politely what they want.
slip away and come back with a roasted calf.
offer water and wait to see if they stay.
fork.reveal: he didn't delay: he went quietly to his household and brought a fat roasted calf, then set it near them. the feast came before any questions.

original.note: Arabic, from Qur'an 51:24: "the honored guests of Ibrahim." dayf means guest.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about angels.
what it means: a story about a host. Ibrahim feeds strangers at once and well, before he knows they carry news of a son.
what a scholar hears: al-mukramin, "the honored": commentators read it both ways, guests honored by Allah and guests honored by Ibrahim's welcome.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 6018; Sahih Muslim 47 (whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honor his guest)
Genesis 18:1–15 (the visit at Mamre, named as a neighbor)

notes: The index word here is the title head "Guests with news" (kept exactly). The hook field avoids naming Sarah because the Qur'an does not; the script says Muslim tradition knows her as Sarah. Confirm.
"Slipped away to his household quietly" renders fa-ragha ila ahlihi (51:26); "so the guests wouldn't feel like a burden" is a common commentary explanation, stated as such. Confirm wording.
Fear at guests who won't eat: explained as a custom of the time (a guest refusing food might mean harm). This is the usual tafsir explanation; confirm.

Why Sarah laughed: the Qur'an's order in 11:71 puts the laugh before the news is stated; commentators differ (relief at the news about Lut's people, surprise, etc.). Script says only that they disagree.
Hadith number for honoring the guest cited from memory (Bukhari 6018/6019; Muslim 47); please confirm.
Trapdoor: the two readings of al-mukramin (honored by Allah / honored by Ibrahim) are given in classical tafsir; confirm.
Review pass: the howItsDone line no longer puts the hadith wording in quotation marks (no translation is cited); it now refers to the hadith about honoring the guest.
